issues.item: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a 21-year-old woman with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, 'being alone with women' is not a clinically coherent trigger unless the crash specifically involved women in a central way. Nothing in the other selected nodes supports a gender-specific interpersonal trauma cue. The rest of the profile is accident-related and self-focused, so this trigger appears mismatched to the trauma context and to the formulation.

issues.item: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent for a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. 'Crash Imagery' fits the trauma, but 'Feeling happy or relaxed' and 'Talking about the future' are unusually abstract/internal states rather than plausible trauma reminders for this event, and together they do not form a believable trigger profile tied to the crash.

issues.item: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: Within the trigger node, the items do not hang together as a consistent reminder pattern. A concrete crash reminder ('Cars hit by accident') is paired with broad positive-affect/future-oriented states that suggest a different mechanism and are hard to reconcile as the same patient's main trauma triggers.

vignette: Maya is a 21-year-old electrician who lives alone in a small town in the Midwest. She started the job at the age of 18, working long hours on residential wiring projects and often driving with her crew to various sites. The day that changed everything was a Saturday morning when she was driving her company van toward a suburban street to pick up a new set of panels. The road was slick with rain, and on the corner ahead, a delivery truck had just been hit by a high-speed car. The impact was sudden and violent; the van, positioned a few feet behind the truck, was forced sideways by a spray of debris. Maya felt the jolt of the collision and heard the crash-echoing as the truck crashed into the pole. Her heart pounded, her breath caught, and the world seemed to tilt. When the ambulance arrived, she was still shaking, eyes wide with disbelief, as paramedics pulled her out of the van. She survived, but the memory stayed, vivid and terrifying. Since that day, Maya has carried a constellation of triggers that feel inescapable. Whenever she hears someone talk about their future plans-especially plans that involve driving or moving away-her mind suddenly replays the collision. The mere sight of cars racing on the highway or even a photograph of a dented bumper brings her breath to a shallow halt. Even in her own garage, when she watches a video of a vehicle crash, her stomach clenches and she finds herself retreating into silence. On the job site, the sight of a coworker's car idling next to her own van makes her glance away, her hands tightening around the steering wheel in a reflexive, uneasy grip. These triggers do not merely remind her of the event; they activate deep, unsettling doubts about herself, about the fairness of her world, and about the reliability of her own body. When a trigger flares, Maya's negative appraisals surface in a swift cascade. The image of a crash forces her to question whether she will ever be able to make the right decision behind the wheel. "I can't trust that I will do the right thing," she tells herself with a tremor. The sense of injustice gnaws at her-"What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it"-echoes whenever she sees the same scene again. And the memory of the van's sudden, unanticipated shift leads her to feel that her own body is no longer a trustworthy partner: "I can no longer trust my own body." These appraisals, each born from a trigger, become anchors that hold her in a state of chronic hyper-alertness. The more she sees or hears about future plans, the more her self-doubt and sense of injustice are reinforced, creating a vicious loop that feeds on itself. In turn, the weight of these negative appraisals pushes Maya toward avoidance that pervades her daily life. The dread of speaking about her future compels her to keep conversations about plans at the job site to a minimum; she steers clear of planning road trips or discussing career moves with friends. When a coworker invites her to drive the van together for a longer job, Maya feels a rising tide of fear that she will make a mistake, that she will not trust her body to keep her safe. Consequently, she either refuses or pulls out at the last moment. The injustice appraisals make her feel that no one will ever protect her or compensate her for the loss of control she experienced, so she actively avoids situations that might expose her to further harm. The cycle is self-reinforcing: avoidance keeps her from confronting her trauma, yet avoidance also keeps the negative appraisals alive, ensuring that triggers will always be the source of her anxiety. Weeks of avoidance have started to take a toll on Maya's professional relationships. Her supervisor notices that she is late on deadlines, citing that she "cannot focus" on her work. Maya blames her own incompetence, reinforcing the self-doubt that she cannot trust herself to make the right choices. The sense of injustice makes her believe that the job environment is unkind and that the company has not provided adequate support after the accident. The feeling that her body is unreliable causes her to experience physical tension during electrical inspections, further impairing her performance. Together, these negative appraisals and avoidance behaviors have created a chain of consequences that strain her relationships at work and isolate her socially. Maya finally decided to seek help after a recent incident at a job site where she was tasked with wiring a new panel in a high-rise building. She was alone in a cramped electrical box, the overhead lights flickering, and the hum of the building's HVAC system pressing against her ears. When a co-worker called her to a different floor, she heard a faint echo of her own breath racing in her chest-a trigger that brought the memory of the crash flooding back. Unable to focus, she made a mistake that nearly caused a short circuit, and her supervisor reprimanded her, saying, "You can't be this careless." The shame, combined with her fear of making the accident again, shattered her sense of competence. That day, the weight of her negative appraisals became unbearable, and she realized she could no longer function safely at work or maintain her relationships. She now seeks therapy to break this loop and to find a way to move forward without being ruled by the fear that has dominated her life since that rainy Saturday. She is most afraid that she will never trust herself again, but she hopes to reclaim her sense of control and to speak openly about her future, no longer haunted by the ghosts of that collision.
